extracted.intended_audience: copyeditors, authors, and publishers (University of Chicago Press / academic editors)
extracted.subtask_description: House-style rules for capitalization, italics, quotations, spelling, and punctuation as used by an academic press; guidance for preparing text, citations, letters, captions, and legal/technical references.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Capitalization in hyphenated compounds in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with the main words capitalized, all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds are capitalized; do not capitalize such components when other than nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Twentieth-Century Progress," "The Economy of High-Speed Trains." But: Fifty-first Street; "Lives of Well-known Authors," "World-Dominion of English-speaking Peoples."

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Capitalize scientific (Latin) names of higher taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological matter, the scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera are capitalized, but their English derivatives are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cotylosauria (but cotylosaurs); Felidae (but felids); Camivora (but carnivores). Also: species names derived from persons or generic names may be capitalized in botanical/zoological contexts; in geological and medical matter species names are never capitalized. See examples (Cocos nucifera, Rosa Carolina; geological exceptions like Pterygomatopus schmidti).

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes should be capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kafir, Negro (in its ethnical sense), Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Capitalize astronomical body names (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical work, capitalize the names of the bodies of our solar system, except the words 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' and 'stars'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. Capitalize institutional divisions/offices in official work
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago are capitalized in all official work dealing with its administration or curricula, with specified lower-case exceptions in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (the University), the School of Education (but: the school), the University Extension Division (but: the division), the Department of Anthropology (but: the department); the Board of Trustees (the Trustees, the Board), Dean of the Faculties (but: the faculty). Also examples of titles: Professor of Physics, Assistant in Chemistry, Van Husen Scholarship (but: the scholarship); courses: First Term (but: two terms; major, minor).

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Use capitals and small capitals for date lines and salutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and signature/residence lines using capitals and small capitals; follow specified indentation and placement conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and formatting: Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911 (set to the right, with one em's indention, preferably in smaller type); 'My dear Mr. Smith:' set flush followed by a colon in same type as body in a separate line. Signature and residence lines set to the right with one em's indention.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Capitalization/format for 'Whereas', 'Note', and 'Section' in formal documents
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'Whereas'; in notes (not footnotes) use 'Note.' followed by a period and dash; in constitutions/by-laws use 'Section' introducing paragraphs followed by a number. 'Section' may be abbreviated after first use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Note. — 'It should be noticed that ...'; Section 1. This association shall be styled ...; thereafter: Sec. 2. The object of the association ...

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Small capitals for era/time abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M. and P.M. and B.C. and A.D. in small capitals and without spaces between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D. (See cross-references 22, 103, 106.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Lowercase originally proper names now common
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a small initial (lowercase) for words of common usage that were originally proper names and their derivatives, where the origin is obscured; generally apply to verbs derived from proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, anglicize, macadamize.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Lowercase minor subdivisions and their abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, minor subdivisions and their common abbreviations are lowercased: chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; abbreviations like chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See other rules (37, 110, 337) for cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Lowercase abbreviations for units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial letters for common unit abbreviations (h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second, lb.=pound, oz.=ounce, yd.=yard, ft.=foot, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metric and customary units as abbreviations in many contexts (see related rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Capitalization in italic side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; set the rest in lower-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for further cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Initial word case for integrated quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation is immediately connected with the preceding text through a conjunction or otherwise, use the same case (usually lower-case) for the first word of the quotation even if the original begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Italicize for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to lend emphasis or importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italicize foreign words and brief foreign passages (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases from foreign languages not incorporated into English, and single sentences or brief passages in a foreign language, unless incorporated or anglicized; do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of institutions/places whose English usage requires roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung'; do not italicize 'Père Lagrange,' 'Freiherr von Schwenau'; do not italicize suffi ciently anglicized words like 'percent', 'personnel', 'resume', 'naive' (list provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italicize titles of publications and certain long works
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of books (including long poems printed separately), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals; also the city in newspaper titles when integral to the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer-Night's Dream; the Modern Language Review; the Chicago Tribune. Note: exceptions in lengthy bibliographies, tables, or where excessive italics would be undesirable; books of the Bible and ancient manuscript titles should be set in roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Italicize certain Latin/legal reference words but not common abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words/abbreviations used in literary and legal references such as ad loc., circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, supra, s.v., vide. Do not italicize of., e.g., i.e., v. or vs., viz., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italics to differentiate traditional scholarly Latin terms; common abbreviations remain roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Italicize 'See'/'See also' in indexes and errata
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics for the words See and See also when used in an index or similar compilation for cross-references, and for 'for' and 'read' in lists of errata to separate incorrect and correct readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: See also Sociology; for levee read levée.

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Italicize party names and certain procedural titles in legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize the names of plaintiff and defendant in the citation of legal causes, and the titles of proceedings containing prefixes like In re, Ex parte, and In the matter of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Formatting and capitalization of address lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, etc., and primary address lines in letters should be set flush in a separate line, with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:'; 'Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Formatting of signatures and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title added after the name follows rules: if one word run into same line; if more than one word but not longer than name center first letter under name line and indent; if longer center name over second line and set second line flush; subject to special-case exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary' (one-word title on same line); 'Carter H. Harrison' then 'Mayor of Chicago' on separate line centered. Practical exceptions allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Use of a), b), c) etc. for subdivisions and fractional verse/page parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c) etc. to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double parentheses if 'run in'); and use a, b, c, etc. affixed to verse/page numbers to denote fractional parts (e.g., Luke 4:31a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply single vs double parenthesis formatting depending on paragraph position.

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Use letters to designate unknown quantities and lines in technical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters (lower or upper case as appropriate) to designate unknown quantities, lines, powers, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ac+bc=c(a+b); lines ad and AD; the nth power.

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Use letters in text to refer to illustration elements
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, use letters in legends or text referring to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations (e.g., 'At the point A above (see diagram)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistent letter usage between figure and text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. Formatting references to particular letters
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to particular letters in text, format them as such: 'the letter u,' 'small v.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear typographic distinction when discussing letters as items.

rubrics_metrics.name: 70. Monetary shorthand following numerals (shillings and pence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use s.2d.d. (= shillings and pence) following numerals in the specified abbreviated form (example: 35s. 6d.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 370 for more on monetary notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 71. Italics and roman for scientific names and astronomical nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, geological, and paleontological matter italicize generic and species names when used together and italicize genera used alone; in botanical matter behave similarly; in medical matter general practice is to print such names in roman. For astronomical matter, modern practice is not to italicize Greek, Latin, and Arabic names of planets, satellites, constellations, and individual stars; likewise do not italicize catalogue designations, Flamsteed numbers, chemical element symbols, Fraunhofer capital letters, spectral-type letters, and hydrogen line designations. When initials express titles of catalogues as such, italicize the initials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Canodectes favosus, Phyteuma Halleri; astronomical examples: Jupiter, Tethys, Lyra, Antares, 8S Pegasi, N.G.C. 6165; catalogue initials like B.D., N.G.C. should be italicized when referring to titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: 72. Use of 'Resolved.' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions set the word 'Resolved.' (see rule 39).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format resolutions with 'Resolved.' as introductory word to clauses. Cross-reference to section on 'Whereas' and resolution wording (39).

rubrics_metrics.name: 73. Indicate continued articles with 'Continued'/'To be continued'
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, as a rule, use the words '—Continued' and '[To be continued]' at the end of articles when they continue in later issues/sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example headline: 'THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY—Continued' and bracketed note '[To be continued]'. See rule 179 for continuation conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 74. Use quotation marks for run-in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put citations of a passage from an author, run into the text, between quotation marks and in roman type ("roman-quote").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 85 for when to set quotations in smaller type instead of using quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: 75. Quotation marks for consecutive quotations from different sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from different authors, or from different works by the same author, following each other uninterrupted by original matter or by any reference to sources (other than a footnote figure) should remain in quotation marks even if reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple short quotations follow directly, maintain quotation marks to delineate each source; exceptions noted in rule 85 for reduced type.

rubrics_metrics.name: 76. Use quotation marks for defined terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Place in quotation marks a word or phrase accompanied by its definition when introduced in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '"Drop-folio" means a page-number at the foot of the page.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 77. Quotation marks for unusual/technical/ironic words
rubrics_metrics.description: Place unusual, technical, ironical, or otherwise marked words or phrases in quotation marks, whether or not accompanied by explanatory words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; She was wearing a gown of 'lobster-colored' silk; This so-called 'man of affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 78. Use quotes for translations of foreign words
rubrics_metrics.description: In translations, place the English equivalent of a foreign word or phrase in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Monumisen R/omische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: 79. Quotation marks to draw attention to particular words/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks to indicate the particular word(s) to which attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'; the name 'Chicago.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 80. Quotation marks for serial titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Set series/serial titles in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters' series; 'International Critical Commentary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 81. Quotation marks for titles of shorter poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of shorter poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.' (See rule 60 for book-length poem policy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 82. Quotations for cited titles of subdivisions and articles; capitalized references for preface/introduction etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters), papers, lectures, sermons, articles, toasts, mottoes. References to Preface, Introduction, Table of Contents, Index of a specific work should be set with capitals without quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Beginnings of the Science ... Vol. I, 'The British School,' chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; The subject of the lecture was 'Japan—Its Past, Present, and Future'; but references like Preface, p. iii should be capitalized without quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 83. Quotation marks for names of ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Set names of ships in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S.S. 'Oregon.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 84. Quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 85. Set long quotations in smaller type
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily set all prose extracts that will make five or more lines in smaller type, and all poetry citations of two lines or more; isolated short prose quotations may be run into text if organically related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced extracts generally omit quotation marks (see rules 86-87). Size reduction guidance in rule 86.

rubrics_metrics.name: 86. Specific reductions for reduced citations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reducing type for quotations, reduce from 11-pt and 10-pt to 9-pt, from 9-pt to 8-pt, from 8-pt to 6-pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 252 for related typographic sizing conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 87. Omit quotation marks for reduced citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations should not have quotation marks, except in cases noted in rule 75; as a rule, do not use quotation marks in connection with italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions exist when clarity requires quotation marks (e.g., adjacent different authors' quotations).

rubrics_metrics.name: 88. Include ellipses and 'etc.' within quotation marks when indicating omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when it would not otherwise be clear that they stand for omitted material; clarity in each case is the controlling criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrast where 'etc.' inside vs outside quotation marks shows whether it belongs to the quoted material or the surrounding text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 89. Repeat opening quotation marks for each paragraph of a broken quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoted prose broken into paragraphs, repeat the opening quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not close the quotation marks at paragraph breaks unless the quotation ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90. 'Clearing' quotation marks for alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alignment is desired, quotation marks should be 'cleared' (i.e., should project beyond the line of alignment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows opening quotation marks projecting before the left aligned text to preserve visual alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 91. Alternation of double and single quotation marks for nested quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotation marks for primary quotations and single quotation marks for a quotation within a quotation; alternate double and single for further nesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The orator then proceeded: 'The dictionary tells us that "the words, 'freedom' and 'liberty'..."' '

rubrics_metrics.name: 93. Spell out titles of honor and certain forms of address
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out all religious, civil, and military titles of honor and respect and forms of address when preceding the name, except certain abbreviations (Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon., St. are exceptions as noted); abbreviate Esq. following the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French forms: M., MM., Mme., Mlle. The Rev. and the Hon. are not set (except in quotations and correspondence).

rubrics_metrics.name: 94. Spell out most small numbers in ordinary reading-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to exceptions, in ordinary reading-matter spell out all numbers of less than three digits unless statistical/technical or in long groups; use figures for decimals, degrees, dimensions, distances, enumerations, money, percentages, weights, and similar technical matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities ...'; but: 'He spent 128 days' or '10^, 45 miles, 9 per cent.' Treat connected groups consistently; if the largest has three or more digits, use figures for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: 95. Spell out round approximate numbers subject to limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out round numbers (approximate figures in even units) using limits: in numbers under 1,000 the limit is 100, and under larger numbers the limit is 1,000; give specific exceptions and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'estimated at five hundred' (but use figures for 550); 'a thesis of about three thousand words' (but use 2,700 if exact). Prefer 'fifteen hundred' rather than 'one thousand five hundred' in special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 96. Spell out numbers that begin sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, no matter how high, commencing a sentence in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out; when impracticable reconstruct the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women, ... went down with the ship.' If impractical, rephrase: 'The total number ... was 593 men.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 97. Spell out isolated sums of money in running text; use figures in statistical lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring as isolated cases in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out; when several such numbers occur close together or in statistical contexts use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The admission was two dollars.' vs 'Admission: men, $3; women, $1; children, 35 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 98. Time-of-day formatting depends on context
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter express time of day in words ('at four', 'at half-past two in the afternoon'); in statistical/enumerative contexts and when used with A.M./P.M. use figures (e.g., 4:15 P.M.), and omit 'o'clock' in such connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow A.M./P.M. small-cap formatting (rule 52) when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: 99. Spell out ages in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Express ages in words in ordinary reading-matter: 'eighty years and four months old; children between six and fourteen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures in statistical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 100. Spell out numbers of centuries, dynasties, sessions, and similar references
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out numbers of centuries, of Egyptian dynasties, of sessions of Congress, of military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares, etc., unless brevity is an important consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session; Fifth Avenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101. Decade references in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to particular decades in running text in words: 'in the nineties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerals when context/statistical precision requires otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102. Spell out names of months in normal prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the names of months spelled out except in statistical matter or long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from January 1 to April 15' (omit the ordinal suffix after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: 103. Use 'United States' spelled out except in specified contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out 'United States' except in quotations and certain abbreviated/formal connections (e.g., military/general abbreviations U.S.A., ship names U.S.S.) and in some footnotes/references (U.S. Geological Survey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references (22, 52, 106).

rubrics_metrics.name: 104. Capitalize Railroad, Fort, Mount, Port in geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: In geographical appellations capitalize words like Railroad (-way), Fort, Mount, and Port as part of proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad (not R.R. or Ry.); Fort Wayne, Mount Elias, Port Huron.

rubrics_metrics.name: 105. General rule: spell out names of publications (with flexibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases spell out the full names of publications in text; this rule is flexible and subject to modification by expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, spell out; good taste tolerates spelling out more than contraction. Exceptions for bibliographies and technical lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: 106. Use specified state abbreviations in lists/bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviate names of U.S. states, territories, and possessions following town names in lists (without space between letters) using a specified set of abbreviations; these are not ordinarily used in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ala., Ariz., Cal., Conn., etc.; use T.H. for Territory of Hawaii, P.I. for Philippine Islands, P.R. for Porto Rico, D.C. for District of Columbia, W.Va. for West Virginia, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 107. Ampersand and firm-name abbreviations in technical bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies) abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use ampersand (&) in commercial firm names (Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.); in nontechnical running text spell such words out unless the firm name itself uses ampersand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If firm name does not consist of proper names, spell out 'and' (American Steel and Wire Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 108. Abbreviate 'Saint' as 'St.' in place names but prefer omission for apostles etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' before place names like St. Louis, St. Peter's Church, SS. Peter and Paul; prefer to omit 'St.' with names of apostles, evangelists, church fathers (Luke, Paul, Augustine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply preference for omission in formal prose unless context dictates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: 109. Standard abbreviations for books of the Bible and versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific standard abbreviations for books of the Old and New Testaments, the Apocrypha, and common versions of the Bible (lists provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gen., Exod., Ps. (Pss.), Matt., Luke, Rev.; Versions: A.V. = Authorized Version; R.V. = Revised Version; A.R.V. = American Standard Revised Version, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 110. Abbreviate bibliographical designations in footnotes and bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical matter abbreviate terms such as Vol., No., Ps., chap., art., sec., p., col., Fig., pp., pp. sf., pp. sff., etc., following their numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I; No. i; Ps. 20; chap. ii; p. 5; pp. 5-7; pp. sff.

rubrics_metrics.name: 112. Modern citation spelling/punctuation vs. original
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling/punctuation differ slightly, adopt house style; in citations from Old English works or where fidelity is essential, follow the original; always quote titles accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial discretion to balance readability and faithfulness to source.

rubrics_metrics.name: 113. Form possessives of names ending in s or sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: For proper names ending in s or another sibilant, form the possessive by adding '’s' if monosyllabic, and an apostrophe alone if the name has more than one syllable; for names ending in a silent sibilant always add apostrophe + s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Bimis's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth; Charlevoix's discoveries, Des Moines's population.

rubrics_metrics.name: 114. Use 'a' vs 'an' based on pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'a' before sounded A, long u (or eu), and the words 'one,' 'once'; use 'an' otherwise (before vowel sounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hotel, a union, a euphonious word; an hour, an honor if pronounced with vowel sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: 115. Avoid ligatures æ and œ in modern usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use ligatures æ and œ in modern English words; write ae or e separately or use e alone; ligatures retained in Old English and French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aesthetic (not æsthetic); oeuvre remains with œ in French; but maneuver (not manœuvre) in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: 116. Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' to mean 'more remote' or physical distance; use 'further' to mean 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: 117. Vocative 'O' vs exclamation 'Oh' punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative) use the 'O' (without comma following); for an exclamation use 'Oh,' followed by a comma or exclamation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!'; 'Oh, why did not Cerberus drag me back to hell?'

rubrics_metrics.name: 118. Retain final -e in specific participles
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final 'e' in their primary words when forming -ing participles (list provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of retaining -e: agreeing, hieing, singeing, dyeing, hoeing, tingeing; contrasted list shows many participles that omit the e, e.g., abridging, acknowledging, aging, arguing.

rubrics_metrics.name: 119. Preferred American spellings for numerous common words
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a long lexicon of the preferred spellings (American) for many common words and variants (e.g., abridgment, accouter, acknowledgment, color, theater, neighbor, organize variants, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is prescriptive for house style; includes 'aluminum' (not aluminium), 'color' (not colour), 'center' (not centre), 'theater' (not theatre), 'program' (not programme) where specified; also notes one-word forms like 'anyone', 'today', 'cannot' and distinctions like 'sometimes' vs 'some time(s)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 120. Preferred -ise vs -ize endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate which verbs are to be spelled with -ise and which with -ize/-yze; extensive lists show the preferred termination for each verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: spell with -ise: advertise, advise, comprise, despise, arise, surprise; spell with -ize (-yze): aggrandize, analyze, baptize, civilize, emphasize, organize, familiarize, modernize, etc. See comprehensive lists for each verb class.

rubrics_metrics.name: 121. Match punctuation style with preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word, letter, or character immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'With the cry of Banzai!' the regiment stormed the hill; Luke 4:16a; No. I.

rubrics_metrics.name: 122. Period usage to end complete sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a period to indicate the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 125 for many exceptions in headings, legends, and certain labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: 123. Period after abbreviations with exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations except where a mechanical necessity omits letters in the middle of a word (indicated by apostrophe) or specific exceptions (e.g., certain recognized abbreviations). Treat metric symbols as abbreviations (with periods) but not chemical symbols nor 'per cent' in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. 1, Chas.; 10 mm. (metric symbol with period in many house examples); exceptions: O, Fe; a per cent; 4to, 8vo. Note further exceptions for some journals (Asirophysical Journal style).

rubrics_metrics.name: 124. No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even when they serve as ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: 125. Omit periods after certain headings and legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, and superscriptions/legends that do not form a complete sentence; also omit after date lines and signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headings and labels without full sentence structure do not take terminal periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: 126. Period placement relative to quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the period inside the quotation marks; place it inside parentheses when the enclosed matter is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tennyson's 'In Memoriam.' (Put the period inside the quotation marks—rule without exception.) When parentheses form part of the preceding sentence, put the period outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: 127. Use the exclamation point for outcries/emphatic/ironic utterances
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the exclamation point to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Long live the king!' 'Heaven forbid!' 'How funny this seems!'

rubrics_metrics.name: 128. Placement of exclamation point relative to quotes/parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the exclamation point inside quotation marks or parentheses when it is part of the quotation/parenthetical matter; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same principle applies to question marks (see rule 129).

rubrics_metrics.name: 129. Interrogation point usage and omission for indirect questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interrogation point to mark a direct query or to express doubt; do not follow indirect questions with a question mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Who is this?' The prisoner gave his name as Roger Crowninshield (? ). Indirect question: He asked whether he was ill. (No '?')
